results.title: Two AWS GPU Price Hikes in Six Months: Rethinking Your AI Compute Mix - Upendra Sengar Blog
highlights:
In early July, AWS raised EC2 Capacity Block prices 20% across its main GPU instance families. That is the second hike in six months, following a 15%…

 August 6, 2026 5 min read Upendra Sengar 

In early July, AWS raised EC2 Capacity Block prices 20% across its main GPU instance families. That is the second hike in six months, following a 15% increase on January 4. If you are on H100-based P5 instances, you are now paying $5.19 per GPU hour. B300 slots hit $14.04 per GPU hour. For a team running a p5e.48xlarge continuously, the January hike alone pushed the bill from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour. The July hike adds another layer on top of that.

...

If you are calling inference APIs, you are paying a fraction of what you paid two years ago. Per-token prices have dropped roughly 80% in 2026 alone and around 280-fold since 2022. Claude, Gemini Flash, and the latest DeepSeek models are all priced in a range that would have seemed impossible eighteen months ago.

But that is API inference. If you are reserving GPU capacity for training runs, fine-tuning, or heavy batch processing, you are in a different market. That market is going up. Demand for training capacity has not softened. Amazon committed roughly $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex this year to keep pace. They are not subsidizing that from goodwill.

The mistake I see teams make is treating these two markets as one question: "should we use cloud GPUs or APIs?" That framing is too coarse. The real question is what kind of compute you are actually buying, and which market it belongs to. AWS announced the July 1 increase in late June, affecting P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de families. If your team missed that, check your bill.

...

Anything that involves gradient updates lives in the capacity block world. You need reserved GPU time in large blocks, and the price just went up again.

A lot of teams I talk to are revisiting whether the fine-tuning step is necessary at all, or whether a well-crafted system prompt with retrieval does 90% of the job. In many cases, it does. Before you book more capacity blocks, run that experiment. The gap between "fine-tuned model" and "strong base model with good retrieval and a detailed prompt" has narrowed, and the compute cost of closing it has widened.

...

AWS will almost certainly raise capacity block prices again. The demand side has not cooled and $200 billion in capex has to get paid back. The teams that come out ahead are the ones who stop treating all GPU spend as one category and start routing workloads to the market that actually fits them.

### What the table tells you

Three things stand out in the August 2026 snapshot. First, the spot spread is huge but narrowing: spot-to-on-demand savings run 28–60%, with Vast.ai and Spheron offering H100 spot at under a dollar an hour. Second, hyperscalers still charge 3–4x the neo-clouds for the same H100 silicon — AWS lists $8.50/hr on-demand against $2.50/hr on Vast.ai/Spheron — so the "AWS price" you see quoted in most headlines is not the market-clearing price. Third, E2E's ₹209/hr deal makes India genuinely price-competitive with the global neo-clouds, which was not true earlier in the year.

## Has the H100 price gone up or down recently?

Over the last few months the H100 on-demand price has been roughly flat, with the significant movement at the margins: spot capacity tightened in July 2026, and on Spheron H100 spot (≈$2.91/hr) briefly traded at or above on-demand (≈$2.54/hr) — a sign that interruptible capacity was scarce enough that the "discount tier" lost its discount. Compared with the May–June 2026 baseline reported in our spot vs on-demand H100 analysis, headline on-demand rates (AWS $8.50, Azure $8.00, GCP $7.50, Lambda $3.49, Vast $2.50) are unchanged, which is itself the story: after the sharp 2025–2026 run-up, on-demand H100 has plateaued. The volatile variable is now spot, and the cheap-tier leader (Vast/Spheron $0.99) is where you'll see the next move if B200 supply keeps pushing H100 demand sideways.

## What is the H100 spot price vs on-demand price right now?

Right now, H100 spot is $0.99/hr on Vast.ai and Spheron, versus $2.50/hr on-demand on those same providers — a 60% saving for interruptible capacity. Across all providers in the feed, spot runs 28–60% below on-demand, with the Neo-cloud spot leaders (Vast $0.99, Spheron $0.99, E2E $1.50, Nebius $1.80) well under half the hyperscaler spot (AWS $5.00, Azure $4.80, GCP $4.50). The catch is preemption: spot instances can be reclaimed when demand spikes, so they suit batch inference, fine-tuning and distributed training that can checkpoint and resume — not real-time services. If your workload must stay up, pay the on-demand rate; the 60% spot saving is real but conditional on interruption tolerance.

India-hosted H100 on-demand rates otherwise run ₹219–400/hr: CloudMinister lists ₹219–250/hr, JarvisLabs lists ₹255.15/hr, and E2E's GPU rental page shows ₹350–400/hr. Two practical notes for Indian teams: first, Neo-cloud spot at $0.99/hr is the true cost floor but comes with preemption risk; second, an India-hosted provider (E2E, JarvisLabs) gives INR billing, lower egress latency, and local compliance, which matters if you are subject to India data-residency rules — see E2E Networks vs Vast.ai for India GDPR.

## Will H100 prices fall when B200 supply increases?

We do not know, and we will not pretend to forecast it. The honest answer is that the relationship between B200 supply and H100 pricing is not currently forecastable from the public data. B200 rental has been volatile in 2026 (averaging ~$5–6/hr through mid-2026, with neo-cloud spot dipping to ~$3.35–3.70/hr while hyperscalers charge up to ~$14/hr), and B200 on-demand is available from $4.50/hr in this month's feed. On one hand, a flood of B200 capacity could relieve H100 demand and pull H100 prices down; on the other, H100 remains the default for many 70B-class workloads the B200 simply isn't needed for, so demand may prove sticky. State a directional guess, not a forecast, and re-check the live table monthly.

## Why H100 prices are up — the 4 structural bottlenecks

H100 rental prices are up roughly 20% year-over-year in 2026, and the trend is driven by supply constraints that are structural, not cyclical:

### HBM3e Memory — sold out through 2026

H100 uses HBM3 (80GB); H200 upgraded to HBM3e (141GB). Both SK Hynix and Micron are sold out through all of 2026, capping GPU output before it even reaches packaging.

### TSMC CoWoS Packaging — 2-year backlog

CoWoS is the bottleneck across NVIDIA's entire data-center GPU lineup. TSMC is expanding but won't catch up until late 2027.

### NVIDIA allocation — hyperscaler priority

NVIDIA prioritizes AWS, Azure, GCP, Oracle and Meta for H100/B200 allocation; smaller providers and brokerages get the remainder and pay premium prices.

### Blackwell transition — allocation-only

B200 is allocation-only in 2026 and priced at $30K–$45K MSRP. NVIDIA is shifting 5nm capacity from H100 to B200, tightening H100 supply even as demand keeps rising.

...

Spot prices will converge toward on-demand. As utilization rises, Vast.ai's spot pool (typically 15–25% of capacity) has already shrunk to 10–15%. Expect H100 spot to approach $1.50–$2.00/hr by mid-2027.

highlights:
# Why Does the Same NVIDIA B200 GPU Cost $3.75/hr on One Cloud and $27/hr on Another? 

If you've been comparing NVIDIA B200 GPU pricing across cloud providers, you've probably noticed something strange.

The exact same NVIDIA Blackwell GPU can cost $3.75/hour on one cloud and well over $20/hour on another.

Same silicon.

Same memory.

Same NVIDIA hardware.

So...

Why are you paying 5-7x more?

The answer isn't the GPU.

It's everything wrapped around it.

You're Not Just Buying a GPU When you launch a B200 instance, you're paying for far more than compute.

Hyperscalers bundle together:

Enterprise networking

Managed infrastructure

Premium support

Integrated storage

Security services

Long-term enterprise SLAs

Those services matter for some organizations.

But if your goal is training models, serving inference, or experimenting with AI workloads, you may end up paying for services you never actually use.

Same GPU. Different Business Model. Neoclouds have changed the economics.

Instead of charging for a massive cloud ecosystem, they focus on one thing:

Delivering NVIDIA GPUs at the lowest possible cost while maintaining performance.

That's why pricing can vary dramatically despite identical hardware.

The GPU inside the server hasn't changed.

The pricing strategy has.

results.title: Self-Hosted LLM Costs 2026 | Pricing Comparison
highlights:
### Cloud GPU Instances (On-Demand and Reserved)

The 2026 cloud GPU market reflects NVIDIA shipping Blackwell-generation hardware alongside still-available Hopper-class instances. On-demand pricing for NVIDIA H200 instances (141 GB HBM3e) runs approximately $4.50 to $6.00 per hour on AWS, GCP, and Azure, with Lambda Labs and CoreWeave offering rates between $3.50 and $4.50 per hour for equivalent configurations. NVIDIA B200 instances, now available in limited regions, command $6.00 to $8.50 per hour on-demand from major hyperscalers, while GB200 NVL2 configurations (2-GPU module; confirm 384 GB combined HBM3e per NVIDIA product page before procurement) price between $10.00 and $14.00 per hour on-demand.

> Note: All cloud GPU prices cited here reflect estimates as of mid-2026. Rates change frequently—consult AWS, GCP, Azure, CoreWeave, and Lambda Labs pricing pages directly before making procurement decisions. On-demand H200 and B200 instance availability is capacity-constrained; production workloads should use reserved instances or maintain fallback capacity.

Reserved pricing changes the picture. One-year commitments typically reduce rates by 30% to 40%, and three-year reservations by 50% to 60%. For running a 70B-parameter model at moderate throughput (~30 to 50 tokens per second for concurrent users), an H200 instance suffices. At a reserved one-year rate of around $2.80 per hour on CoreWeave, monthly cost lands at $2,016 for continuous operation.

### Dedicated Server and Colocation

Bare-metal GPU server rentals from providers like Hetzner, OVH, and specialized GPU hosts offer a middle path. Monthly pricing for a server with a single NVIDIA A6000 Ada (48 GB VRAM) runs $400 to $700, while configurations with dual or quad H100 SXM GPUs range from $4,000 to $10,000 per month depending on provider and contract length.

results.title: Spot GPU Droplets vs On-Demand GPU Droplets | DigitalOcean Documentation
highlights:
# Spot GPU Droplets vs On-Demand GPU Droplets (public)

DigitalOcean Droplets are Linux-based virtual machines (VMs) that run on top of virtualized hardware. Each Droplet you create is a new server you can use, either standalone or as part of a larger, cloud-based infrastructure.

GPU Droplets are available with on-demand or spot capacity. Both tiers provide the same GPU configurations, but they differ in availability, pricing, and the possibility of reclamation.

Note:

Spot GPU Droplets are in public preview. Spot GPU Droplet pricing is separate from on-demand pricing and may change daily based on available idle GPU capacity.

| On-Demand GPU Droplets | Spot GPU Droplets |
| --- | --- |
| Guaranteed capacity. After you create an on-demand GPU Droplet, its capacity remains available until you destroy it. | As-available capacity. Spot GPU Droplets use available idle GPU capacity, so DigitalOcean does not guarantee availability. |
| Fixed pricing. On-demand GPU Droplets have a fixed hourly rate. | Variable pricing. Spot GPU Droplets always cost the same as or less than the equivalent on-demand GPU Droplets, but pricing may change daily based on available capacity. Check the current rate in the DigitalOcean Control Panel. |
| No capacity-based reclamation. DigitalOcean does not reclaim on-demand GPU Droplets to reallocate capacity. | Capacity-based reclamation. DigitalOcean may reclaim a Spot GPU Droplet with at least two hours’ notice. We send the notice by email to both the team account and the account that created the Droplet. |
| Stable workloads. On-demand GPU Droplets are best for production, latency-sensitive, or stateful workloads that require continuous capacity. | Fault-tolerant workloads. Spot GPU Droplets are best for fault-tolerant workloads that can save progress, restart, and move to another instance. |

results.title: Cloud GPU Pricing War 2026: CVM vs AWS vs Azure vs DigitalOcean - Tencent Cloud
highlights:
The cloud gpu pricing landscape in 2026 is crowded and noisy. Providers list hourly rates, per-second rates, reserved and spot variants, and committed-use discounts, and they often quote different GPU models at different memory tiers. Two numbers that look comparable on a pricing page can describe very different things once you account for the card underneath, the memory attached, and the network around it.

The backdrop includes upward pressure on hardware costs. DigitalOcean has publicly raised GPU instance prices, and that kind of move ripples through the market and shows up in list prices over time. The point of raising it here is not to judge the move — providers set prices for their own reasons — but to flag that any snapshot of pricing goes stale, and the right way to compare is by method rather than by a single number you saw once.

...

A honest gpu cloud comparison 2026 starts with the dimensions, not the dollar signs. If you compare on hourly rate alone you will pick the wrong provider, because hourly rate hides the GPU model, the memory, and whether the price includes the host CPU and storage.

| Dimension | Why it matters | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GPU model and generation | Same price, very different throughput | Is it an A100, H100, or older card? |
| GPU memory | Determines max model size and batch | GB per card, and whether shared |
| vCPU and host RAM | Feeds the GPU; undersized host bottlenecks | Cores and GB included in price |
| Local storage type | NVMe vs network-attached affects data loading | Is fast local disk included? |
| Network bandwidth | Multi-node training and large model pulls | Egress and east-west bandwidth |
| Billing granularity | Per-second vs per-hour changes short jobs | Minimum charge and rounding |
| Spot / reserved options | Same instance at very different cost | What discount for what commitment |
| Region availability | Cheapest region may lack the GPU you need | Is the instance in your region? |

The table is the comparison. Once you have filled it in for each provider, the "cheapest" answer usually changes by workload — and that is the correct outcome. A provider that

...

With the dimensions set, here is how the four providers line up. The instance families are public; the prices below are approximate list prices as of writing and are shown to give shape, not precision. Always verify on the provider's own pricing page before deciding, because cloud gpu pricing moves.

| Provider | Representative GPU instance family | GPU class | Approximate on-demand pricing shape | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CVM | GPU-enabled CVM instances | Mid-range to high-end | Pay-as-you-go + reserved options | Standard Linux server model; SSH, Docker, CUDA toolkit |
| AWS | P4/P5 family (e.g., p4d, p5) | A100 / H100-class | High hourly; significant reserved discount | Mature ecosystem; per-second billing on many types |
| Azure | NC/ND series | A100 / H100-class | Comparable hourly; reserved and spot available | Enterprise integration; broad region footprint |
| DigitalOcean | GPU Droplet | Single-card, mid-range | Recently raised; simpler pricing | Smaller catalog; developer-focused experience |

Read the table as shape, not verdict. The CVM row lists a pay-as-you-go and reserved model without pinning a specific monthly fee, because the right figure depends on the instance type and region you select. The AWS and Azure rows are in the same band for high-end cards, with their differences showing up in commitment discounts and ecosystem. DigitalOcean sits in a different niche — fewer instance types and a recently raised price that reflects its smaller catalog.

...

For steady, committed workloads, the deciding factor is the discount curve. AWS and Azure offer meaningful reductions for committed use, and CVM has its own reserved options — so a fair comparison prices the same job under each provider's commitment, not just the on-demand rate. The methodology is the same either way: pick the job, fill in the dimensions from the table, price it under the billing model that matches your usage, and compare. Anything shorter than that is a guess. To anchor that guess in real numbers, the CVM product page lists the GPU instance types and billing models you can price against.
